paragraphs.source_en: Interesting similarities may be found between the San rain animals and the Round Head down-headed animals. They are both indeterminable as a species and apparently very similar in form. The San rain animals are killed in order to bring rain. Lewis-Williams (1981; 2004) notes that in rock art dying animals and especially the eland are represented in a posture in which their head is markedly downwards as a sign of difficulty in standing because of the oncoming death. The same position of difficulty is also evident in the Round Head down-headed animals. Can we therefore suppose that they are also representations of dying animals? And if so, can we suppose that these indeterminable quadrupeds also represent rain animals, the death of which is the necessary condition for the rain to come?

paragraphs.source_en: Another parallel is the frequency of these animals. In the South African rock art there are often only one or a few, frequently large and prominent, rain animals in a rock shelter, whereas there are large numbers of depictions of eland (Lewis-Williams & Pearce 2004). It is exactly the same situation in the Round Head art where there are only around 20 depictions of down-headed animals compared with circa 300 antelope and mouflon. The relatively small number of rain animals in South Africa is explained by the fact that the painted image was a manifestation, an embodiment, of the rain man's particular rain-animal. Among the San, rain controllers are men and each of them operates with his own animal (Lewis-Williams & Pearce 2004).

paragraphs.source_en: Comparing the South African rock art and its ethnography, I suggest that the down-headed animals present in the Round Head art may also be rain animals. They are depicted both on the Tassili Plateau and in the lower mountains, namely the Algerian Tadrart and the Tadrart Acacus. It indicates that these creatures were a generally known and used concept which may be explained by the constant necessity, in all African societies, to assure the rain. Rain is regarded by traditional African societies as a sacred phenomenon, sometimes intimately associated with God (Mbiti 1969). It would be rather surprising if such a complex society producing the Round Heads ignored this fundamental notion both in their ideology and in their rock art. The down-headed animals could be the testimony of ancient rain-making rituals occurring in the Round Head sites.
